tpl:g10m1s3-1-2:exactly-one-rational: judge: solution_ok is False — The arithmetic is right in all three instances. The keys are C, A and B, giving 7/2, 3/2 and 9/7. The cube facts are right: 7^3=343, 3^3=27, 9^3=729, 25 lies between 8 and 27, 14 between 8 and 27, and 63 between 27 and 64. Exactly one option is rational in each instance. Every tagged distractor is irrational and fits its misconception, and the stem is unambiguous. I set solution_ok to false because of the worked-solution reasoning, not the keys. (1) Step 3 argues "pi is not an integer, so it is not a fraction of integers", then says "the top and the bottom must both be integers". That is a non sequitur and a false test for a number. 0.6/2 or (3/2)/4 have non-integer tops but are rational, and the family's own step 2 has to simplify the cube root to 7 before the top becomes an integer. A student can learn "numerator not an integer as written means irrational". The valid argument is that if pi/4 were rational then pi = 4*(pi/4) would be rational, which contradicts pi being irrational. (2) Step 4 asserts that pi^n "cannot be simplified to a fraction of integers" with no reason. The claim is true, but a Grade 10 student has no basis for it, and it invites the false rule that a power of an irrational number is irrational (sqrt2^2 = 2 is a counterexample). The step should lean on the stem's guarantee that exactly one is rational, or cite the book's statement about powers of pi, instead of asserting it. Fix: rewrite steps 3 and 4 with the multiply-back argument or an explicit "exactly one is rational, so the rest are irrational" justification, and drop the "top and bottom must both be integers" sentence. The distractors, key form and context need no change.
tpl:g10m1s6-1-3:expand-unit-binomial-tri:
judge: key_form_ok is False — Mathematics is correct in all three instances. I expanded each product independently: g003 gives x^3 - 5x^2 + 7x - 12, g005 gives x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6, and g009 gives x^3 + x^2 - 13x + 3. Each marker key and answer_check is the same expression as that result, and every worked solution reaches it correctly. Each solution multiplies by the binomial's first term, then its second term, lists all six products, collects like terms and writes the answer in descending powers, and every sum in step 4 is right. The stems are plain expansions with no word problem, so context_ok is true. The family has no multiple-choice options, so distractors_ok is true and the list is empty.

key_form_ok is false for presentation only. The stem asks for the answer in its simplest form, but the displayed LaTeX key writes negative middle coefficients as '+ (-k)x': g003 'x^{3} + (-5)x^{2} + 7x - 12', g005 'x^{3} + (-2)x^{2} + (-5)x + 6', g009 'x^{3} + x^{2} + (-13)x + 3'. A student shown this key as the model answer could learn '+ (-5)x^2' as acceptable simplest form. The answer_check strings are fine and need no change because they are machine-side. The fix is to regenerate the displayed key with signs merged, as in x^{3} - 5x^{2} + 7x - 12, x^{3} - 2x^{2} - 5x + 6 and x^{3} + x^{2} - 13x + 3. I answered false because the instructions say to reject when in doubt.

misconceptions.label: Checks the top of a fraction instead of its denominator
misconceptions.description: The student tests the top of the fraction for the problem, so either misses a zero denominator because the top looks fine, or treats a zero on top as if it were division by zero.

misconceptions.label: Reads a minus sign in front of a root as a minus sign under it
misconceptions.description: The student sees a minus sign next to a square root, as in $-\sqrt{15}$, and treats it as the square root of a negative number, so calls it non-real (or undefined).

misconceptions.label: Swaps the labels non-real and undefined
misconceptions.description: The student sees that the number is a special case but treats non-real and undefined as one idea, so calls the square root of a negative number undefined, or a fraction with a zero denominator non-real.

misconceptions.label: Rational only if it comes out neat
misconceptions.description: The student calls a fraction of integers, or a decimal whose digits repeat, irrational because it does not work out to a whole number or a decimal that stops.

misconceptions.label: Root sign means irrational
misconceptions.description: The student sees a root sign and calls the number irrational without first working out whether the root comes out as an integer.

misconceptions.label: Uses perfect cubes to locate a square root
misconceptions.description: The student finds the two perfect cubes either side of the number under a square root and takes their roots as the two integers, instead of using perfect squares.

misconceptions.label: Treats a square root as half the number
misconceptions.description: The student takes the square root of a number to be about half of that number, so places the root next to half the number under it instead of finding the perfect squares either side.

misconceptions.label: Uses perfect squares to locate a cube root
misconceptions.description: The student finds the two perfect squares either side of the number under a cube root and takes their roots as the two integers, instead of using perfect cubes.

misconceptions.label: Adds the numerators and adds the denominators
misconceptions.description: The student writes one fraction whose numerator is the sum of the numerators and whose denominator is the sum of the denominators, instead of first making the denominators the same.

misconceptions.label: Multiplies only part of the numerator by the number the denominator was multiplied by
misconceptions.description: When rewriting a fraction over the lowest common denominator, the student multiplies the denominator and the $x$-term of the numerator by the number needed, but leaves the other number in the numerator as it was, as if the multiplier did not apply to the whole numerator.

misconceptions.label: Multiplies the denominator but not the numerator (or the whole number)
misconceptions.description: When rewriting a term over the lowest common denominator, the student multiplies the denominator by the missing factor but leaves the numerator, or a whole-number term, as it was.

questions.stem: Consider the following list of numbers: $-\frac{3}{5}\;;\;\sqrt{-28}\;;\;18\;;\;-\sqrt{2}\;;\;0\;;\;\frac{3}{0}\;;\;-16\;;\;\pi$ The special sets are the natural numbers $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, the whole numbers $\mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$ and the integers $\mathbb{Z} = \{\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$. How many of the numbers in the list are natural numbers?

canonical_solution.text_md: Recall the three special sets: the natural numbers $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, the whole numbers $\mathbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$ and the integers $\mathbb{Z} = \{\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$. All three contain only real numbers, and only whole values with no fraction part.
$\sqrt{-28}$ has a minus sign under the square root, so it is non-real. $\frac{3}{0}$ is divided by zero, so it is undefined. Neither of them can be in any of the three sets.

$-\sqrt{2}$ has its minus sign outside the root, so it is real, but it lies between $-2$ and $-1$, so it is not an integer. The number $\pi$ is real and lies between $3$ and $4$, so it is not an integer either. Neither of them is in any of the three sets.
$-\frac{3}{5}$ is a fraction that is not a whole value, so it is real but not an integer, and it is in none of the three sets.
$18$ is a positive integer, so it is a natural number (and therefore also a whole number and an integer).
$0$ is zero, so it is a whole number (and an integer), but it is not a natural number.
$-16$ is a negative integer, so it is an integer, but it is neither a whole number nor a natural number.
The natural numbers are the positive integers, because the set starts at 1.
Counting the numbers in the list that are natural numbers gives 1.

Round $i$ to $2$ decimal places. The digits up to decimal place $2$ are kept and the next digit is $5$ . A digit of $5$ or more rounds the last kept digit up by $1$ ; a smaller digit leaves it as it is. So $i\approx0.01$ .
Use the rounded value of $i$ in the formula, without rounding again until the end: $\begin{aligned}A&=P(1+i)^{n}\\&=10000\left(1+0.01\right)^{4}\\&\approx10406.0401\end{aligned}$
Round $A$ to $2$ decimal places: $A\approx10406.04$ .
For comparison, working with the unrounded value of $i$ all the way through gives $A\approx10208.27$ , so rounding $i$ early changed the answer by $197.77$ .

Since $343 < 348 < 512$, taking cube roots gives $7 < \sqrt[3]{348} < 8$.
So $\sqrt[3]{348}$ lies between $7$ and $8$.

questions.stem: Estimate the following surd to the nearest $1$ decimal place, without using a calculator. $\sqrt{154}$

canonical_solution.text_md: Find the perfect squares on either side of $154$: $12^{2}=144$ and $13^{2}=169$.
Since $144<154<169$, $\sqrt{154}$ lies between $12$ and $13$.
The two squares are $169-144=25$ apart, and $154$ is $154-144=10$ above $144$. So $154$ is $\frac{10}{25}\approx0.4$ of the way from $144$ up to $169$.
$\sqrt{154}$ is about the same fraction of the way from $12$ to $13$, so $\sqrt{154}\approx12+0.4=12.4$.
Therefore $\sqrt{154}\approx12.4$ to the nearest $1$ decimal place.
